scenes.headline: Joins
scenes.subtitle: Combining two DataFrames on matching keys.
scenes.narration: A join combines two DataFrames by matching rows on a shared key, letting you bring related data together.

scenes.headline: Join essentials
items: Match rows using a join key and condition
Choose a join type: inner, left, right, or outer
Joins are wide operations that trigger a shuffle
Broadcasting a small side avoids the shuffle
scenes.narration: You match rows using a join key and pick a join type such as inner or left. Joins are wide operations that trigger a shuffle across the cluster, though broadcasting a small side can avoid that shuffle entirely.

scenes.headline: Common join types
scenes.narration: An inner join keeps only rows that match on both sides and is the most common. A left join keeps every left row, and an outer join keeps both sides, filling any missing matches with nulls.

scenes.headline: An inner join on a key
scenes.code:
result = orders.join(
    customers,
    on="customer_id",
    how="inner")
result.select("order_id", "name", "amount").show()
scenes.narration: We join orders with customers on the shared customer id using an inner join, so only orders with a matching customer remain. Then we select a few columns from the combined result to display the enriched order records.

scenes.headline: Broadcasting the small side
scenes.code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

result = orders.join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
scenes.narration: When one side is small, we wrap it in broadcast so Spark ships a full copy to every executor. This turns the join into a shuffle-free broadcast join, which is dramatically faster than shuffling the large orders table.

scenes.text: Broadcast the small table to skip the shuffle — but only when it truly fits in memory.
scenes.narration: Broadcasting the small table skips the expensive shuffle, but only do it when that table genuinely fits in executor memory.
